move: Give your slowest day 1 recurring reason to visit, such as a weekly dish or a game, and run it every week without skipping.
why: A fixed weekly reason lets guests build a habit around your quietest day, which fills seats you already pay to staff and light.
example: If the weekly event adds 25 covers spending $30 each, that is $750 more in sales each week.
watch: Judge it on the trend over several weeks, since a new habit builds slowly and the opening week tells you little.
follow_up: What theme would suit my slow day?
basis_note: Quill (owner reported): a Latin kitchen's Monday date night lifted sales 24% in its 1st year and its taco Tuesday became its 3rd busiest day, though both used discounts. FSR 2025 (Toast data): early week reservations are rising, so promote the quieter room. Chowhound citing Toast 2024: only 6% of reservations fall on Monday nights.

move: Before you discount your slow day, count how many guests using the deal already came in at full price.
why: Some of every discount goes to guests who would have paid full price anyway, and deal seekers rarely return at full price.
example: If 60 of 80 deal guests are regulars who each save $6, you give away $360 to people who were coming anyway.
watch: Compare total sales on deal days with the same days before the deal, rather than counting redemptions.
follow_up: What should I do instead of discounting?
basis_note: Thompson (Cornell, early bird and night owl specials): estimate cannibalization from full fare guests who take the special instead. Dholakia (Rice, 324 businesses): only 19.9% of daily deal users returned at full price, only 35.9% spent beyond the deal, about 80% were new customers, and only 43.6% of restaurants profited. Kimes found targeted specials can lift revenue, so the move is to measure before discounting.

move: Pull 8 weeks of hourly sales and consider closing, or opening later, during the hours that never cover their staff and running costs.
why: An hour that brings in less than it costs to stay open loses money every time, so cutting it can raise profit on fewer sales.
example: If your last hour sells $90 and costs $140 to staff and run, closing it saves $50 a day.
watch: Tell regulars before you change hours, and check whether their visits shift into your other hours.
follow_up: Which hours are worth closing?
basis_note: US Foods Food Fanatics (Datassential data): the average restaurant is open 6.4 fewer hours than in 2019, and an Atlanta chef who now closes 2 days a week says she makes as much money with shorter hours. NRN 2022: independents cut 7.5 weekly hours on average. 5280: staffing drove many cuts. No study of the revenue effect was found.

move: Offer your slowest block to a local group that meets regularly, such as a club or a professional association, with a reserved area and a short set menu.
why: A group that meets regularly brings a known headcount on a day you staff anyway, and the booking repeats.
example: A 12 person club spending $18 each brings $216 into a block that might have sat empty.
watch: Ask the organizer to confirm numbers the day before, and keep the group menu to dishes you already prep.
follow_up: How do I find local groups to host?
basis_note: FSR 2017: become a meeting point for local groups by contacting organizers, since groups meet regularly and bring repeat business. Quill: office parties and professional association meetings fill slow periods. Run clubs and book clubs were not verified.

move: If you want a slow day offer, make it a short fixed price menu at set hours rather than a discount across the whole menu.
why: A narrow offer limits how much full price business it eats into, and the kitchen preps a short, predictable list.
example: If 3 courses cost you $11 in ingredients and sell together for $35, each set brings $24 toward your other costs.
watch: Build it from dishes you already prep, or the savings disappear into extra prep labor and waste.
follow_up: How should I price a set menu?
basis_note: Thompson (Cornell, early bird and night owl specials): estimate how much full fare business a special cannibalizes before offering it. Kimes via the Post-Bulletin: time based price differences are acceptable when framed as savings. Quill: fixed price dinners that require reservations fill slow nights. No source compares a slow night set menu directly with a straight discount.

move: If you run a happy hour, set it in your slowest hours and lead with food specials built from items you already prep.
why: A happy hour placed when you are already busy only discounts guests who would have come anyway.
watch: Compare total sales in those hours before and after you start, rather than counting happy hour orders.
follow_up: What should go on a happy hour menu?
basis_note: Restaurant Dive 2024: happy hours help drive traffic during slow periods of the day. NRN 2011: a cafe chain ran $5 small plates in a nonpeak window to spur traffic. SpotOn: use the hourly report to find slow periods before you start. Many states restrict alcohol discounts, so the move is food led.

move: Offer remote workers a weekday package for your quiet hours, such as a reserved table, coffee and wifi at a flat daily or monthly price.
why: Remote workers fill seats that would sit empty in quiet hours, and a set price makes their stay pay.
watch: Limit laptop seats at your busy times, so meal guests can still find a table.
follow_up: Should I limit laptops in my cafe?
basis_note: FSR 2017: offer new solo business owners a private table, free coffee, wifi and a quiet place to work for a monthly fee, and become a meeting point for local groups. 1 trade source, no outcome data.

move: During your busiest hours, run a shorter menu built from the items that sell most and that the line can make fastest.
why: Fewer items mean fewer stations juggling at the same time, so tickets come out faster and you serve more guests while demand is highest.
watch: Keep your best sellers on the short menu, and brief staff before service so every guest hears the same explanation.
follow_up: Which items should I keep during the rush?
basis_note: NRN 2017: a casual chain trimmed nearly 50% of its menu and ticket times fell 12%, with tickets over 15 minutes down 40%, though traffic also fell in the same 3 months. The Takeout 2019: a burger chain CEO planned to pare the menu to speed service. Kimes at Chevys: some restaurants run only special menus at peak holiday periods. Evidence comes from whole menu cuts at chains.

move: Set a prep par for each item by day of the week from your sales history, and have it ready before the rush starts.
why: Running out mid rush slows every ticket and loses sales, while prepping too much turns straight into waste.
watch: Adjust the pars weekly from what was left at close and what ran out early.
follow_up: How do I set prep pars?
basis_note: 7shifts forecasting guide: sales history can predict how many of each item you will sell in a shift. 7shifts inventory guide: a par is the minimum you need on hand, so make or order the gap. Restaurant365: forecast production from comparable periods to cut waste. No source covers prep pars by weekday directly.

move: Cap how many covers you book in each 15 minute slot so orders reach the kitchen in waves it can handle.
why: When too many tables order at the same time, tickets back up and every table waits, which slows the whole room.
watch: Watch ticket times in the busiest slots, and lower the cap wherever they climb.
follow_up: How many covers per slot can my kitchen take?
basis_note: Resy: pacing caps covers per time increment, default 10 covers every 15 minutes, and online bookings obey it. FSR 2019: flow controls pace tables so the kitchen does not back up. Hostme: per slot cover caps in 15 to 60 minute increments to balance floor and kitchen. Set the cap from measured kitchen output.

move: When the line reaches the door, send a 2nd staffer along it with a handheld or order pad to take orders and payment.
why: People leave lines that do not seem to move, and taking orders early keeps them from walking away.
watch: Make sure the bar or kitchen can keep pace, or the wait just moves to the pickup counter.
follow_up: How long a line makes people leave?
basis_note: US Foods (written by the Toast team): line busting means staff work up the line taking orders on handhelds, with a trigger rule such as 10 or more people waiting, and a cafe cut rush ticket times to about 8.5 minutes. Starfleet Research with Square 2025: 68% of operators use handhelds for line busting or tableside ordering (sponsored).

move: Give online pickup orders their own shelf or table away from the register, with each order clearly labeled.
why: Pickup guests skip the line, the cashier keeps serving walk ins, and the counter stops clogging at peak.
watch: Check that orders do not sit long on the shelf, and set ready times the kitchen can actually hit.
follow_up: How do I keep online orders from swamping the rush?
basis_note: Foodservice Equipment and Supplies 2022 and 2023: give pickup its own shelves near the kitchen or cashier and keep pickup traffic out of the dining room. QSRweb 2016 (Olo): pickup customers get stuck in checkout lines, so keep the lines separate with signage and order throttling.

move: Put 1 person at the pass during the rush whose only job is to call tickets, check each plate, and send it out complete.
why: An expediter keeps tickets moving in order and catches mistakes at the pass, which holds kitchen times steady as covers climb.
watch: Put your clearest communicator at the pass, and count remakes before and after.
follow_up: Who on my team should run the pass?
basis_note: Kimes at Chevys: managers added an expediter on the middle line during hot periods and the kitchen held order to entree times steady at about 11.5 minutes despite more covers, alongside other changes. FE&S 2022: separate expediter stations for dine in and to go.

move: Batch your busiest drinks before the rush, such as cold brew, iced tea or house syrups, so each order goes out fast.
why: Drinks built from scratch at peak slow every order behind them, and batching also makes each drink taste the same.
watch: Batch only what a normal peak sells, and note what is left at close to set the next batch.
follow_up: How much should I batch each day?
basis_note: Perfect Daily Grind 2025: with concentrates an iced latte takes about 1/3 of the time. VinePair: batching is almost essential for speed of service (cocktail context, same principle). Cocktail batching itself was left out of the playbook because pre-mixing spirits is restricted in some states.

move: Time a busy service from seating to payment and shorten the idle gaps, such as waiting for menus, orders or the check, instead of rushing guests.
why: Guests resent being hurried while they eat but rarely notice shorter waits for service, so trimming the gaps frees tables without hurting the meal.
watch: If reviews start mentioning feeling rushed, you trimmed the wrong part of the meal.
follow_up: Where do meals lose the most time?
basis_note: Kimes at Chevys: most slack sat in the steps before and after the actual meal, and managers did not want guests to feel rushed while eating. Noone et al. 2007: do not rush the meal itself, satisfaction with that part matters most. Kimes, Wirtz and Noone: guests accept or do not notice trims at the start and end of a meal (student sample).

move: Bring the check soon after plates are cleared and guests pass on dessert, and let them pay at the table.
why: Waiting for the check and the card can take a real share of a meal, and those minutes hold a table nobody is enjoying.
watch: In fine dining, wait for guests to ask for the check, since a check that arrives too early can sour the meal.
follow_up: Should I get handheld card readers?
basis_note: Kimes at Chevys: check drop to departure took about 19% of a 53 minute meal (our arithmetic), servers were trained to drop the check when clearing entrees, and check drop to settlement fell from 5:40 to 2:55. Noone et al. 2007: speed at check settlement is appreciated even where speed during the meal is not. Susskind and Curry (Cornell 2016): pay at table devices cut table time about 15%, though about 25% of guests dislike them.

move: Count your party sizes for a month, then set out enough tables for 2 and for 4 to match the parties you actually get.
why: A party of 2 at a 4 top leaves 2 seats empty every time, and the right mix seats more guests in the same room.
example: If 10 parties of 2 a day sit at 4 tops, that is 20 empty seats you could have sold.
watch: Keep some tables that push together for larger groups.
follow_up: How should I lay out my room?
basis_note: Kimes at Chevys: about 70% of parties were 1 or 2 people in a room of mostly 4 tops, a better table mix with the same seats raised busy period occupancy from 50% to 59%, alongside other changes. Cornell Chronicle 2003 (Thompson): small combinable tables suit small independents with small parties. SevenRooms quoting Kimes: seating 2 at a 4 top compounds on busy nights.

move: When the room fills up, have servers clear finished plates during the meal and assign 1 person to reset each table as guests leave.
why: A dirty empty table is lost seating while guests wait at the door.
watch: Clear only plates guests are clearly done with, since grabbing too early makes them feel rushed.
follow_up: How fast should a table be reset?
basis_note: Kimes at Chevys: departure to bussed took 2:48, mainly from no prebussing, and prebussing plus a dedicated scraper and stacker at busy times cut it to 2:00. Noone et al. 2007: rushing the meal itself hurts satisfaction, so prebus with care.

move: If you need time limits at your busiest times, state them when guests book and explain why, or use set seating times instead.
why: Many guests dislike time limits, and a limit explained in advance feels far fairer than a surprise at the table.
watch: Never pull a table that is still eating, and offer a counter seat to guests who want to stay on.
follow_up: How long should each booking get?
basis_note: Kimes (Cornell survey): maximum duration policies were rated unfamiliar and not acceptable, 54% of comments were negative, and she suggests set seatings and making the policy familiar. Wirtz and Kimes 2007: framing matters most when a policy is unfamiliar. McGuire and Kimes 2006: explaining a policy improves perceived fairness. Disputed, so the move offers set seatings as the alternative.

move: If servers walk every order to a terminal, try handheld devices that send orders straight to the kitchen and take payment at the table.
why: Orders reach the kitchen sooner and servers stay on the floor, so each server can cover more tables and the meal moves faster.
watch: Some guests dislike paying on a device, so keep a server ready to run the card the usual way.
follow_up: Are handheld devices worth the cost?
basis_note: FSR 2023: a breakfast and lunch chain timed its service and reported that handhelds cut ordering time 3.6 minutes per group and let servers handle 12% more tables (operator reported). Susskind and Curry (Cornell 2016): tabletop payment cut table time about 15%, though about 25% of guests dislike the technology and a co-author worked for the device maker. Starfleet with Square 2025: 82% of operators reported faster service (sponsored).

move: Train staff to suggest 1 named item that fits the order, such as a side or a drink, instead of asking if guests want anything else.
why: A specific suggestion gives guests an easy yes, while a vague question invites a quick no.
example: A $5 side added to 1 in 5 of 400 checks a week is $400 a week.
watch: Suggest what suits the order rather than the priciest item, or guests feel pushed.
follow_up: What should my staff suggest?
basis_note: FSR (Restaurant365 author): replace a generic anything else with a specific suggestion tied to the order. Van Kleef et al. 2015 (Wageningen): when cashiers named 1 side at breakfast, orange juice went from 20% of orders to 35 to 42%, and surveyed guests did not feel pressured. Toast warns against pestering.

move: Keep small treats by the register and have staff offer 1 that fits the order, like a cookie with a coffee.
why: A small item offered right at payment is an easy yes, and it adds to the check with almost no extra work.
example: A $3 cookie added to 1 in 10 of 1,000 weekly orders is $300 a week.
watch: Rotate what sits at the register and note which items actually sell there.
follow_up: Which items sell best at the register?
basis_note: Van Kleef et al. 2015: cashiers naming 1 item at a self service breakfast counter lifted that item share of orders. Toast: the fastest win is 1 relevant high margin add on recommended every time with the related item. No cafe test of register displays was found.

move: Show every table the dessert menu or a dessert tray instead of asking if they saved room.
why: Guests turn down a question about dessert far more easily than a dessert they can see.
example: If 1 in 5 of 300 weekly covers adds an $8 dessert, that is $480 a week.
watch: At times when guests are waiting for tables, a slow dessert course can cost a turn, so offer it to go.
follow_up: Which desserts sell best?
basis_note: Avero (2015): always drop a dessert menu and point to a favorite. Toast: present dessert before the check and track dessert attachment. St. Louis Magazine 2024: in busy mid priced rooms an extra 30 minutes for dessert can earn less than another turn. Practitioner advice, no controlled test.

move: Have servers suggest 1 shareable appetizer for the table right after the drink order.
why: A shared appetizer is eaten while mains cook, so it adds to the check without slowing the table.
watch: Send it quickly so it lands well before the mains, or it can hold up the table.
follow_up: Which appetizer should we suggest?
basis_note: ICE (restaurateur Rick Camac): offer a starter with the opening round of drinks, 12 oysters at $3 split by 4 adds about $9 a person. BCcampus textbook: a starter is eaten during the normal kitchen wait, so it adds revenue without lowering turnover. Operator guidance, no controlled test.

move: Set your online ordering and any kiosk to suggest 1 relevant extra with each main item.
why: A prompt appears on every order without fail, and guests often add more when they can browse without a line behind them.
watch: Keep it to 1 prompt per item, since a string of pop ups slows ordering and annoys guests.
follow_up: Which extras should my online menu suggest?
basis_note: University of Hamburg 2023: kiosk customers at fast food restaurants spent 14% and 16% more, credited to consistent cross selling and less social pressure. NRN 2018: operators say kiosk checks run higher because they upsell every time. NPR 2012 (McDevitt): the same customers online pizza orders were 4% pricier. Contrary: a 2019 UNT thesis found kiosks brought in less at 1 burger chain.

move: Build a combo that joins a main with a side and a drink at a small saving over buying them separately.
why: Many guests pick a combo even for a small saving, and it adds a higher margin side and drink to orders that would have been a main alone.
example: If a $9 sandwich becomes a $13 combo on 100 orders a week, sales rise $400 a week.
watch: Check that combos add items guests were not already buying, since a combo that only discounts their usual order lowers profit.
follow_up: How big a saving should a combo give?
basis_note: Duke (Sharpe and Staelin 2010): people preferred combos even with no discount and 26% enlarged their meal when offered 1. Kasavana (AHLEI part 3): value meals raise the average check. Toast: check whether a bundle adds sales or only discounts what guests already buy. QSR cites NPD data that value bundles drove visits more than check size.

move: Raise prices by small amounts more often, a few items at a time, instead of 1 large jump across the whole menu.
why: Small steps keep pace with costs while guests barely notice, whereas a big jump sends regulars comparing.
example: Adding $0.50 to an item that sells 200 a week brings in $100 a week.
watch: Track each item's count after a change, and hold the price on any item whose sales clearly drop.
follow_up: How often should I raise prices?
basis_note: NRA piece (pricing consultant Craig Singleton) suggests raises of 3% or 5% every 3 months and warns against a panicked across the board hike. Resy cites the NRA, 3% several times instead of 15% in 1 go each year. Toast: incremental increases land better than big jumps. Conflict: a Modern Restaurant Management roundup quotes a vendor who prefers 1 larger increase.

move: Cost each dish down to the oil and herbs, then set its price so the plate cost lands near your target food cost percentage.
why: Pricing from cost keeps every item paying its share, and most restaurants aim for food cost near 28 to 35% of the menu price.
example: A plate costing $4 at a 30% target prices at about $13.33, so $13.50 fits.
watch: Recheck plate costs whenever supplier prices move, since an old costing hides a shrinking margin.
follow_up: What food cost should I aim for?
basis_note: Toast: price equals plate cost divided by target food cost, most operators target 28% to 35%. Restaurant365: 28% to 35%. JWU and Lightspeed give the same 28 to 35% range. Restaurant Business: many aim for 30 to 35%, the root of the 3 times markup rule. Conflict: Toast lists quick service lower (20 to 25%) while Restaurant Business says QSR often runs higher, and MarginEdge argues a flat 3x markup misprices many menus.

move: When costs rise, raise prices most on signature dishes guests cannot find elsewhere, and least on the familiar staples that bring people in.
why: Guests know what a common dish costs around town, so those prices draw notice, while a dish only you make has more room to move.
watch: Check each item's sales after the change as well as your total.
follow_up: Which items can take a bigger increase?
basis_note: NRA (Singleton): leave prices on key traffic drivers alone, the most popular staples are the most price sensitive. Kasavana (AHLEI): commodity items found on many menus have restricted pricing, signature items unique to you can be priced more flexibly. NRN 2011: a sandwich chain moved to item pricing so it could raise only items with rising costs.

move: Print menu prices as plain numbers, such as 14 rather than $14.00, without dollar signs.
why: Dollar signs remind guests they are paying, and plain numbers can nudge spending up a little.
watch: Use the same plain style on every menu and board so prices look consistent.
follow_up: What else on my menu affects what guests spend?
basis_note: Cornell Center for Hospitality Research (Yang, Kimes, Sessarego 2009): lunch guests given numeral only prices spent more than those shown dollar signs or written out prices, about 8% more per the Cornell Chronicle (201 diners). 1 lunch field test, not replicated. Toast menu design tips also say drop the dollar sign.

move: Put a price on every extra that costs you money, such as an extra shot, added protein or extra sauce.
why: Free extras quietly raise your food cost on every order that takes them.
example: Charging $1 for added protein on 150 orders a week brings in $150 a week.
watch: Keep extra prices fair and leave a small free touch or 2, so guests do not feel nickel and dimed.
follow_up: What should I charge for extras?
basis_note: Toast: show add on prices clearly and confirm each add on margin covers its food and prep cost. Lightspeed: upcharge for add ons. Retail Dive: a taco chain app orders averaged 20% above in store, partly from paid extras. Alternative milk was left out on purpose: large coffee chains dropped that charge in 2024 to 2025 and it drew disability discrimination suits.

move: Before any price change, write down what 3 nearby places charge for items like your 5 best sellers.
why: Guests compare you with the places they could walk to, and those prices show where you have room.
watch: Compare portion and quality too, since a bigger or better plate can carry a higher price.
follow_up: Should I match the cheapest place nearby?
basis_note: Johnson and Wales: check your largest competitors menu prices. NRA (Singleton): know whether your prices are comparable or too low. Resy cautions against simply undercutting since low prices can signal lower quality, and an NRN 2011 piece prefers pricing from your own history.

move: When costs rise, build the increase into your menu prices rather than adding a surcharge or fee at the bottom of the check.
why: Guests read the menu price as the price, so a fee they meet at payment feels like a surprise and can cost you their goodwill.
watch: If you already add a fee, read reviews and comments for complaints about it before deciding to keep it.
follow_up: How much can I raise prices before guests notice?
basis_note: NRA (Singleton) advises raising the plate price marginally rather than adding surcharges. Fee disclosure rules vary by state (California hidden fee rules per the state Attorney General), which is why the owner text gives no fee mechanics.

move: If your prices differ by day or hour, present the gap as a saving at quiet times rather than a surcharge at busy times.
why: Guests accept a lower price at quiet times far more readily than a higher price at busy times, even when the gap is the same.
watch: Keep any time based price difference small and clearly posted, so regulars do not feel caught out.
follow_up: Should I charge more at my busiest times?
basis_note: Kimes (Cornell) in the Post-Bulletin 2012: diners were fine with prices varying by time and day, and 20% cheaper during the week was more acceptable than 20% more on the weekend. Thompson (Cornell) citing Wirtz and Kimes 2007: customers view discounts more favorably than premiums, and specials need a cannibalization estimate.

move: Pull 3 months of item sales and plate costs, then sort each dish by how often it sells and how much it earns after food cost.
why: Popular dishes that earn little and slow sellers that earn a lot need different fixes, and this sort shows which is which.
watch: Compare dishes within the same menu section, since appetizers and mains sell at very different rates.
follow_up: What should I do with each group?
basis_note: Kasavana (AHLEI, co-creator of menu engineering with Smith at Michigan State, 1982): popularity is high at 70% of an equal share of the category, profit is high at or above average contribution margin, giving stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs (retain, reprice, reposition, remove). Restaurant Business and the BCcampus open textbook give the same playbook.

move: When you choose which dishes to push, compare the dollars each plate leaves after food cost rather than its food cost percentage.
why: A pricier dish with a higher food cost percentage often leaves more money per plate than a cheap dish with a low percentage.
example: A $24 steak with $9 of food leaves $15, while a $16.50 chicken dish with $4.50 of food leaves $12.
watch: Recheck plate costs before pushing a dish, since a stale costing can make a weak dish look strong.
follow_up: Which of my dishes earn the most per plate?
basis_note: Kasavana (AHLEI): pushing low food cost items often lowers average check and gross profit, so rank items by contribution margin. BCcampus textbook example: chicken at $16.50 and 27% food cost earns $12.00 while steak at $24.00 and 38% earns $15.00.

move: Put the dish you most want to sell at the start or end of its menu section.
why: Items at the start and end of a list get noticed and ordered more often than those buried in the middle.
watch: Move 1 dish at a time and compare its sales over a few weeks.
follow_up: Does the top right corner of the menu matter?
basis_note: Dayan and Bar-Hillel (Judgment and Decision Making 2011): items at the start or end of a category were ordered more, about 20% more in a cafe field test. NRN 2012 on Sybil Yang eye tracking: no sweet spot in the top right, diners read menus like a book, which answers the follow up.

move: Remove dishes that both sell rarely and earn little, starting with any that need ingredients nothing else uses.
why: Each slow dish ties up stock, prep time and line space, so cutting it reduces waste and speeds the kitchen.
watch: Tell regulars when a favorite is leaving, and point them to something close.
follow_up: How many items should my menu have?
basis_note: FSR: long menus raise waste and strain staff, cut items that are hard to make or earn poor margins. QSR (King-Casey): fewer ingredients mean less spoilage and better buying, fewer recipes mean faster prep and fewer errors. NRN 2017: a casual chain cut 30 to 40% of items to speed service. FastCasual 2026 notes the growth edge of small menus has faded, so trimming saves cost but does not by itself bring traffic.

move: Describe the dishes you want to sell by how they taste and how they are made, instead of a plain list of ingredients.
why: Guests order with their appetite, so naming flavors and cooking methods makes a dish more tempting than a dry list of ingredients.
watch: Taste words only help when the dish lives up to them, so fix weak recipes before rewriting their descriptions.
follow_up: How long should menu descriptions be?
basis_note: Turnwald et al. (Psychological Science 2019): across 5 university dining halls, taste focused labels raised vegetable selection 29% vs health labels and 14% vs basic labels, with no effect where recipes were the weakest. APS news note: vague hype words fail. The often quoted 27% figure traces to Wansink and was not used.

move: When traffic falls, find out who stopped coming and why before you add new dishes to the menu.
why: A new dish adds stock, prep and room for errors, and it only pays off if it brings in guests you were not already getting.
watch: If you do add a dish, retire another so the menu does not keep growing.
follow_up: What actually brings new guests in?
basis_note: NRN 2015: a burger chain added 10 items in 2012 and sales fell, then rose after trimming, and a burrito chain CFO said a new item must bring new customers or more visits. NRN 2017: casual chains diluted themselves adding items to suit everyone. Contested: some chains grew by adding items, and the evidence is chain level.

move: Rerun your item sales and margin sort at least every 6 months, and again whenever a key ingredient price jumps 10% or more.
why: Costs and tastes move, so a dish that earned well last season can quietly turn into a loss.
watch: Change a few items at a time so you can tell what caused any shift in sales.
follow_up: What should I track for each dish?
basis_note: Kasavana (AHLEI): revise the menu 2 times a year, track every 3 months, and re-verify recipe costs each time. Toast: review prices at least 2 times a year and when a key ingredient rises 10% or more. Restaurant Business: menu engineering is an ongoing task.

move: Cost every recipe on a written card down to the oil and the herbs on top, and update it whenever a supplier price changes.
why: You cannot price or control a dish whose true cost you do not know, and small items add up across many plates.
example: An uncounted $0.40 sauce cup on 500 plates a week is $200 a week of hidden cost.
watch: Check that the line follows the card, since a correct costing means little if portions drift.
follow_up: What food cost should I aim for?
basis_note: Gordon Food Service: do not forget toppings, sauce and packaging, food costs are not static, $0.08 of oil a plate at 50 plates a day is $1,460 a year. Restaurant365: cost every recipe and update as vendor prices change. Lightspeed: most operators keep food cost between 28 and 35%. Contrarian note: MarginEdge says tiny items can be skipped for a rough margin.

move: Count inventory at the same time each week and compare what you actually used with what your sales say you should have used.
why: The gap between actual and expected use reveals waste, heavy portions or loss that a monthly total hides.
watch: Count the same way every week, with the same person if possible, so the numbers compare fairly.
follow_up: How big a gap is normal?
basis_note: FSR: count weekly on the same day before deliveries arrive. MarketMan: same day, same time, same people. Restaurant365: the gap between actual and theoretical comes from portions, waste, bad counts and price changes, best in class is about 1% or less, and a small gap matters more than a low percentage.

move: Give every station scales, scoops and ladles sized to each recipe, and post a photo of each finished plate.
why: Small overportions on popular dishes add up to real money over a week.
example: An extra ounce of a $0.50 an ounce protein on 300 plates a week is $150 a week.
watch: Spot check plates during service, since tools only help if the line uses them.
follow_up: How do I get cooks to portion consistently?
basis_note: FSR: color coded scoops give portion control and speed, plus scale checks. Gordon Food Service: over portioning cheese by $0.20 a plate at 50 plates a day loses $3,650 a year. Clover: recipe cards should include plating notes and a photo of the finished dish.

move: Keep a waste log beside each bin where staff note what gets thrown out and why, and review it every week.
why: Tracking shows the few repeat causes, like overprep or spoilage, and fixing them usually pays back many times what it costs.
watch: Keep logging quick and blame free, or staff will stop writing things down.
follow_up: What causes the most kitchen waste?
basis_note: Champions 12.3 (WRI, 114 restaurants): the average restaurant saved $7 for every $1 invested in cutting kitchen waste, most paid back within a year. ReFED: tracking waste could cut food costs 2 to 6%, pen and paper works for independents. EPA: log amount, type and reason by the bin and use it to adjust menus, buying and portions.

move: Write down what is left in the case at close each day, and bake less of anything that keeps coming back.
why: End of day leftovers are the clearest sign of overproduction, and trimming those batches cuts waste without emptying the case.
watch: Keep the case looking full with smaller batches through the day instead of 1 big morning bake.
follow_up: How much should I bake each day?
basis_note: ReFED restaurant guide: for displayed foods like pastries, put out just enough to look appealing and adjust production from end of day leftovers. EPA food loss checklist: reduce batch sizes and cook closer to demand.

move: Ask guests whether they want bread, chips or an automatic side before bringing it, instead of putting it on every table.
why: Items set down by default often go uneaten, and asking ahead cuts that waste without taking anything away from guests who want it.
watch: Offer it warmly so guests do not feel you are holding back, and watch plate waste before and after.
follow_up: Should I charge for bread?
basis_note: EPA food loss checklist: do not automatically put bread or chips and salsa on the table, ask guests before serving, and ask before serving a side. ReFED: diners leave on average 17% of the food on their plate.

move: Get prices from at least 2 suppliers on your 10 biggest spend items every few months.
why: Prices drift upward when nobody compares them, and a small saving on your biggest items adds up fast.
example: Saving $0.20 a pound on 300 pounds of chicken a week is $60 a week.
watch: Compare cost per usable portion, since trimmed product can cost more per pound but less per plate.
follow_up: How do I negotiate with my supplier?
basis_note: xtraCHEF: target your most purchased items for competitive bids, prices for the same item vary widely. Lightspeed: compare suppliers and negotiate. UNL Extension checklist: send requests for proposals and verify prices against past orders. FSR 2016 notes pre trimmed chicken costs more per pound but removes trim waste.

move: Check every delivery against the invoice for weights, counts and prices before anyone signs for it.
why: Short weights and wrong prices are easy to miss, and you pay for them unless someone checks.
watch: Note every shortage on the invoice and get a credit before the driver leaves.
follow_up: What else should I check on deliveries?
basis_note: Modern Restaurant Management (David Scott Peters): weigh product out of its packaging and ice, compare to the invoice, get a credit memo before signing because a signed invoice is owed as written. UNL Extension: re-weigh weight based items and cross check prices. 7shifts: resolve discrepancies before signing.

move: Build each schedule from expected sales by hour, using the same day in recent weeks, instead of copying last week's schedule.
why: A schedule tied to expected covers stops you paying for idle hours on slow shifts and running short on busy shifts.
watch: Adjust for events, holidays and weather, and compare forecast with actual sales each week.
follow_up: How many staff do I need per shift?
basis_note: Restaurant365: strong operators forecast sales by daypart and build schedules around expected demand rather than templates. FSR (Kristi Turner): historical sales trends take the guesswork out of scheduling. 7shifts: divide forecast sales by your target sales per labor hour to get a labor hour budget.

move: Stagger start and end times so staff arrive as covers build and leave as they fall off.
why: Bringing everyone in at the same time pays for standing around before the rush and after it.
example: Starting 2 servers 1 hour later on 5 days at $15 an hour saves $150 a week.
watch: Keep enough people on to set up and to close properly.
follow_up: How do I schedule around a short rush?
basis_note: FSR (Turner): staggering start times lets labor rise as sales rise through the day. FSR 2023: have 1 person start at 3:00 and another an hour later.

move: Divide sales by labor hours for each daypart to get sales per labor hour, and staff each block to that number.
why: Sales per labor hour shows which shifts are over or under staffed in a way a monthly labor total cannot.
example: If lunch brings $1,800 in sales over 40 labor hours, that is $45 per labor hour.
watch: Compare each daypart with its own history, since busy and quiet blocks will never match each other.
follow_up: What is a good sales per labor hour?
basis_note: 7shifts: total sales divided by total labor hours, use net sales and all paid hours, set targets by daypart, benchmarks roughly $50 to $80 full service, $80 to $120 fast casual, $100 to $150 quick service. Restaurant365: set optimal SPLH by daypart, high may mean understaffing and low overstaffing.

move: Cross train each staffer on 2 stations, such as host and runner or prep and dish.
why: Cross trained staff let you run a leaner crew on slow shifts and cover gaps without calling in extra people.
watch: Train during slow hours, and check that each person can really run the extra station alone.
follow_up: Which roles should I cross train?
basis_note: FSR (Turner): cross training gives flexibility, a busser who can run food. FSR 2023: hosts can bus tables. 7shifts: cross training covers breaks, sick days and swaps.

move: Schedule fewer people through the lull between your busy periods, and have the outgoing shift set up the line so the next crew can start later.
why: Paying a full crew through a predictable lull is a common labor leak, and a ready line lets the next shift start closer to the rush.
watch: Keep enough people on to handle a surprise group, since a lull that suddenly fills can sink service.
follow_up: How many people do I need in a lull?
basis_note: FSR (Turner): flags the mid afternoon lull between lunch and dinner as a place to cut staff. 7shifts: setting up the line before a shift ends lets cooks arrive later. No source said to move prep into lulls, so that idea was dropped.

move: Work out labor cost as a percentage of sales every week and compare it with the typical range for your type of venue.
why: Most counter service places aim for labor near 25 to 30% of sales and full service rooms near 30 to 35%, so check anything well above that.
watch: A very low number can mean you are short staffed, which costs you sales and good people, so look at service too.
follow_up: What labor percentage should I aim for?
basis_note: 7shifts: quick service and fast casual 25 to 30%, casual and full service 30 to 35%, fine dining 35 to 40%, and under 28% may signal understaffing. Lightspeed and FSR put table service at 30 to 40%. Conflict: NRA 2025 data show actual 2024 medians above these targets, 36.5% full service and 31.7% limited service, including benefits.

move: Hold a short huddle before every shift, 5 to 15 minutes, covering the specials, items that are out, and 1 thing to focus on.
why: Staff who know the plan sell the specials with confidence and stop promising dishes the kitchen has run out of.
watch: Vary what you cover, since reading the same list every day makes staff tune out.
follow_up: What should a preshift meeting cover?
basis_note: 7shifts: pre-shift meetings typically run 5 to 15 minutes at the same time every shift, covering announcements, a teaching moment and praise. NRN 2017: a well known fine dining operator calls pre-meal the most important 30 minutes of the day, and operators warn against reading the same list every time. Netchex: announce items that are out and when they return.

move: Thank staff for specific things you saw them do, during the shift and in front of the team.
why: Recognition costs nothing, and staff who feel noticed tend to stay, which saves the cost of hiring and training replacements.
watch: Keep praise specific and spread it across roles, including the kitchen and dish.
follow_up: How do I keep good staff?
basis_note: Gallup with Workhuman 2024 (about 3,500 employees, all industries): well recognized employees were 45% less likely to have changed jobs 2 years later, and WBUR reported the same study. 7shifts: lack of manager recognition is among the top 3 reasons workers left restaurant jobs, and 68% of restaurant workers say regular feedback and recognition make them more likely to stay.

move: Post schedules 2 weeks ahead and keep each person's shifts as steady as you can from week to week.
why: Predictable hours make it easier for staff to plan their lives, and people with steady schedules tend to stay longer.
watch: Set a clear way for staff to swap shifts so last minute changes do not all land on you.
follow_up: How far ahead should I post schedules?
basis_note: 7shifts: 2 weeks ahead is a scheduling best practice, and a restaurant group requires it of managers. University of Chicago randomized trial in retail stores: stable, consistent schedules with easy shift swaps raised sales 7% and labor productivity 5%. Harvard Shift Project: schedule instability strongly predicts turnover among retail and food service workers. Some cities set scheduling notice rules, which are not covered in owner text.

move: Match each new hire with a strong staffer for their early shifts, using a written list of what they need to learn.
why: Many new hires leave in their early weeks, and a structured start keeps more of them, saving the cost of hiring again.
watch: Check in with each new hire at the end of their 1st and 2nd weeks and ask what was unclear.
follow_up: How long should training take?
basis_note: NRA: match each new hire with a buddy, plan day 1 in writing, and check in at the end of week 1. NYC Small Business Services restaurant buddy guide: weekly check-ins in weeks 1 to 4. SHRM Foundation (Bauer): 50% of hourly workers leave new jobs within 120 days, and new hires given structured orientation at 1 manufacturer were 69% more likely to stay up to 3 years.

move: When hiring, look for warmth, curiosity and work ethic, and plan to teach the technical skills on the job.
why: Technical skills can be taught on the job, while natural warmth toward guests is far harder to train.
watch: Ask candidates how they handled a difficult guest, and notice how they treat your staff during the visit.
follow_up: What should I ask in an interview?
basis_note: Danny Meyer (NRN 2007, Global Leadership Network 2018, CNBC 2025): hire 51 percenters, people whose emotional skills such as kindness, curiosity, work ethic, empathy, self awareness and integrity outweigh technical skill, which can be taught. Hiring criteria must stay job related.

move: Have staff taste every new dish before it goes on the menu, and let them describe it in their own words.
why: Staff recommend what they have tasted with more confidence, and their descriptions sound real to guests.
watch: Schedule tastings when the kitchen has time, such as before opening.
follow_up: How do I train staff on the menu?
basis_note: Modern Restaurant Management: daily pre-meal tastings so servers can describe dishes. NRN 2017: a chef has staff taste something at each pre-meal. Restaurant365: a chef table tasting for new hires builds menu mastery and confidence. Drinks were left out of the move because staff alcohol tastings are restricted in many places.

move: Ask your best staff every few months what keeps them here and what would make them leave.
why: Replacing a good worker costs far more in hiring, training and lost speed than keeping them, so their reasons for staying are worth knowing.
watch: Act on at least 1 thing you hear, or the next conversation will be less honest.
follow_up: Why do restaurant staff usually quit?
basis_note: SHRM (Finnegan): stay interviews ask why people stay and what would make work better, kept separate from reviews. 7shifts: more 1 on 1s would affect the happiness of over 2 in 3 restaurant workers. MRM citing Cornell (Tracey and Hinkin): replacing a frontline worker cost about $5,864, 52% of it lost productivity (2006 hotel data, newer operator estimates are lower).

move: Send a confirmation when a booking is made and a reminder the day before, with an easy way to cancel.
why: Many no shows simply forgot or changed plans, and an easy cancel gives you time to rebook the table.
watch: Track your no show rate before and after, by day and by party size.
follow_up: What else cuts no shows?
basis_note: Kimes (Cornell, 816 diners): restaurants can remind guests or ask them to reconfirm, and should make it easy to cancel or report lateness. Zonal with CGA 2023: venues that send reminders see far lower no-show rates. CGA 2021: 27% of no-shows tried to cancel but could not reach the venue and 23% forgot. No typical no-show rate is stated because sources disagree (recorded rates run from about 2% to 5% per booking, survey figures differ).

move: Ask for a card to hold bookings for large parties and your busiest slots, with a clear cancellation window.
why: A hold makes guests take the booking seriously, and a no show on a big table leaves a lot of seats empty.
watch: State the policy plainly at booking, and use judgment with regulars who cancel for real reasons.
follow_up: How much should a no show fee be?
basis_note: Kimes (Cornell): card guarantees were rated the 2nd fairest of 5 no-show policies. Kimes in FSR 2024: guests reacted no differently to a $5 or $25 fee, and those who had seen guarantees were more comfortable with them. SevenRooms: use deposits for large parties, peak times and events. Large parties no-show less often but lose many covers when they do (Resos 2026).

move: Keep a notify list for booked out times and offer each canceled table to it right away.
why: A table that cancels late is lost unless someone is ready to take it.
watch: Respond quickly, since guests on a notify list book elsewhere fast.
follow_up: How do I fill last minute cancellations?
basis_note: Resy: a notify list can refill a late cancellation in minutes. Restaurant Dive 2021: availability alerts are among the standard no-show tools. Resos 2026: backfill gaps from a digital waitlist rather than overbooking. Overbooking was left out of the playbook on purpose because the evidence is thin and it shifts risk onto guests.

move: Keep some tables out of the booking system for walk ins, especially at the counter or bar.
why: Walk ins make up a good share of guests at many places, and a fully booked room turns all of them away.
watch: Track walk ins turned away and held tables left empty, and adjust how many you hold.
follow_up: How many tables should I hold back?
basis_note: Resy help: set some tables to walk in only. NRN 2007 on Kimes and Wirtz: casual restaurants cannot entirely abandon walk ins. Tse and Poon 2017: walk in rates by weekday and meal set the right booking limit. No source gives a share of tables to hold, so the watch says measure your own.

move: Ask guests when they book whether they are celebrating anything, and pass it to the team before they arrive.
why: A celebration changes what guests expect, from a slower pace to a small touch, and knowing in advance lets the team get it right.
watch: Make sure the note actually reaches the server before the guests sit down.
follow_up: What small touches work for celebrations?
basis_note: Kimes, Wirtz and Noone (Cornell): expected meal length depends on the reason for dining, anniversary diners rushed through in an hour may feel short changed. Typsy: tell the team about special occasions in the pre-shift. Resy and Toast 2026: being remembered is what many diners value most. No source measures a spend effect.

move: Set booking lengths by party size from how long each size really stays, instead of 1 length for every table.
why: Small parties usually finish sooner than big parties, so matching durations fits more bookings into the same room.
watch: Recheck actual durations from your booking system every few months and adjust.
follow_up: How long do parties of 2 usually stay?
basis_note: Resy: turn times are the average time each party size dines, from seated to finished. FSR 2019: booking systems set turn times by party size or table, occupancy can range from 45 minutes to 4 hours. Kimes at Chevys: collect a month of POS data on party mix and dining duration before setting policy.

move: Quote waits honestly, leaning a few minutes long, and seat guests before the time you gave.
why: Guests judge a wait against what they were told, so beating a fair quote feels good while running past a short quote feels like a broken promise.
watch: Pad only a little, since an overly long quote sends guests elsewhere, and track how often you beat your quotes.
follow_up: How do I quote wait times accurately?
basis_note: Maister (Psychology of Waiting Lines): some restaurants quote longer than the expected wait so guests are happy to be seated early, satisfaction equals perception minus expectation. University of Cincinnati 2020: pessimistic wait estimates beat optimistic estimates in call center data. Wisely: abandonment rises sharply with long quotes, so padding must stay small.

move: Take a phone number and text guests when their table is ready so they can wait nearby instead of at the door.
why: Guests free to wait somewhere comfortable feel the wait less than guests standing at the door, and your entrance stays clear.
watch: Hold the table for a set number of minutes after the text, and tell guests that rule up front.
follow_up: How long should I hold a table after texting?
basis_note: Toast support: hosts text guests when the table is ready, and a party that does not respond within 15 minutes is closed out. SevenRooms 2020: guests get a text near the top of the list. Maister: occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. No outcome data on walkaways.

move: Hand menus to waiting guests so they choose while they wait and can order as soon as they sit.
why: Idle waits feel longer than occupied waits, and guests who have already chosen order sooner, which shortens the meal.
watch: Have the server greet these tables quickly, since guests who are ready to order notice delays more.
follow_up: What else makes a wait feel shorter?
basis_note: Maister: handing out menus to people waiting in line is common practice, occupied time feels shorter, and waits before service feel longer than waits during it. Noone, Kimes, Mattila and Wirtz (Cornell 2007) list filling waiting time, such as with menus, among ways to manage perceived waits.

move: When a wait runs over, tell guests why and give them a new time instead of leaving them guessing.
why: Unexplained and open ended waits feel longer, and a quick update keeps guests from walking out.
watch: Check on waiting guests at a set interval so nobody feels forgotten.
follow_up: Should I give waiting guests something free?
basis_note: Maister: unexplained waits feel longer than explained waits and uncertain waits feel longer than known waits. McGuire and Kimes (Cornell 2006): explaining a waitlist policy improved perceived fairness in every case. Kimes: knowing how long the wait will be gives guests a sense of control.

move: Let guests join your waitlist online before they leave home, with an honest estimate of the wait.
why: Guests who join from home arrive closer to their table time, which shrinks the crowd at the door.
watch: Explain the policy at the door, so walk ins do not see online joiners as cutting the line.
follow_up: Will an online waitlist upset my walk ins?
basis_note: SevenRooms 2020: guests add themselves to the waitlist from home and track the wait. Toast support: guests join through an online link, and no-shows are closed out after 15 minutes. NRN 2007 on Kimes and Wirtz: call ahead seating was rated relatively fair if easy to explain.

move: Have the host mark every party that leaves the waitlist before being seated, along with the time they were quoted.
why: Walkaways are covers you lose without seeing it, and counting them shows whether long quotes or too few seats are the problem.
example: If 8 parties of 3 walk away each week and each guest spends $25, that is $600 a week lost.
watch: Look for patterns by hour and by quote length, then fix the slot where most guests leave.
follow_up: How long will guests wait before leaving?
basis_note: Wisely: abandonment increases substantially with wait time, so track who left and compare with quote accuracy. Kimes at Chevys: reneging, guests on several waitlists who take whichever table comes up soonest, was a cause of low occupancy. Toast support: the waitlist history logs parties that left.

move: Keep short notes on regulars in your POS or booking system, like their usual order or favorite table, and share them before service.
why: Being remembered is what many guests value most, and notes let any staffer greet them like a regular.
watch: Keep notes about preferences only, and never write anything you would not want the guest to read.
follow_up: What should guest notes include?
basis_note: Resy and Toast Regulars Report 2026: 48% of surveyed diners say being remembered by staff makes them feel most valued, and only 30% say they consistently get it (KEYT reports the same survey). Fortune 2016: guest profiles let even a new employee greet a guest by name. Stored guest data falls under privacy rules, which is why the watch keeps notes to preferences.

move: Start a simple stamp card that earns a free item, and hand out new cards with 2 stamps already filled in.
why: Guests visit more often as a reward gets closer, and a card that starts partly filled feels closer to the goal.
example: If 30 guests a month earn a free $4 coffee, the program gives away $120 a month at menu price.
watch: Track how many members return each month, and keep the rules simple enough to explain in a sentence.
follow_up: What reward should my loyalty program give?
basis_note: Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng (Journal of Marketing Research 2006, a university cafe): purchases sped up about 20% approaching the reward, and a 12 stamp card with 2 stamps prefilled was finished faster than a plain 10 stamp card needing the same purchases. Paytronix via FSR: members spend about 6% more per visit (vendor, members self select). Toast via KEYT 2026: enrollment lifted 90 day return rate from about 7% to nearly 30%.

move: Give new guests a reason to come back soon, such as a card for a dish on their next visit within 30 days.
why: Each return visit makes the next more likely, and a new guest is easiest to bring back while the visit is fresh.
watch: Count how many cards come back, and make the offer something you are proud to serve.
follow_up: How do I turn new guests into regulars?
basis_note: Bloom Intelligence (vendor, 2026): the chance of a next visit rises with each visit, from about 19% after the 1st to 47% after the 2nd, and 42% of returners come back within 30 days, so reach out within a month. Morning Advertiser 2013: hand out bounce back vouchers with the check. Vendor figures are inconsistent, so no return rate is stated to owners.

move: Give staff a small weekly allowance of free items to hand to regulars at their discretion, instead of a standing discount.
why: A surprise from someone who knows them feels personal and costs little, while a standing discount soon feels like the normal price.
watch: Cap the allowance and log each free item in your POS, so the cost stays small and visible.
follow_up: How often should I comp regulars?
basis_note: TIME and HuffPost UK 2015: a sandwich chain lets staff give away a set number of free drinks and food each week to customers they like, about 28% of customers get something free, and it skipped a loyalty card. Resy and Toast 2026: diners value being remembered over points. Points programs also lift visits, so this puts recognition ahead of discounts without ruling them out.

move: Check each month what share of your guests are repeat visitors, using your POS or loyalty data.
why: A small share of regulars drives a large share of sales, and a falling repeat rate can warn of a problem before total sales show it.
watch: Track your own trend rather than a benchmark, since cash guests often go uncounted.
follow_up: How do I get more guests to come back?
basis_note: Bloom Intelligence: measure the share of guests who make each next visit every 3 months, and in its data 5% of new guests who reached 5 visits made 43% of visits. Paytronix via The Wise Marketer: the top 10% of loyalty members made over 50% of loyalty spend. Resy citing Toast: up to 50% of order volume can come from 7% of guests. Benchmarks are vendor defined, so none is given to owners.

move: Check your map and search listings each month for correct hours, special hours and menu link, and add fresh photos regularly.
why: Many guests look you up before visiting, and wrong hours or stale photos send them to the place next door.
watch: Update holiday and special hours early, since showing open while closed sends guests away annoyed.
follow_up: What photos should I post on my listing?
basis_note: Google Business Profile help: keep info complete, including special hours, and add photos regularly. Google claims complete profiles get more visits but cites no study. TouchBistro 2024 (1,500 US diners): 64% search for a restaurant before a new visit and 85% look at the menu online.

move: Post a clear phone photo of a specific best seller on social media shortly before people decide where to eat.
why: Clear, informative food photos tend to do more than polished shots, and a specific dish gives followers a concrete reason to come in.
watch: Social posts mostly reach younger guests, so ask new guests what brought them in before spending more time on it.
follow_up: What should I post on social media?
basis_note: Zhang and Luo (Management Science, via INFORMS 2022): informative photos, especially of food, related to restaurant survival more than photo aesthetics. NapoleonCat (2015 posts): engagement peaks near meal times. TouchBistro 2024: 60% of diners say social media does not influence where they eat, while 48% of Gen Z say Instagram does.

move: Collect opt in emails at the counter and with online orders, and send 1 short note a month with 1 reason to visit.
why: A list reaches guests who already like you at almost no cost, without depending on social media reach.
watch: Send only when you have real news, and watch unsubscribes to know when to slow down.
follow_up: What should I put in my emails?
basis_note: TouchBistro 2024: 53% of US diners prefer to hear from restaurants by email, 33% would unsubscribe over too many or irrelevant emails, and monthly or a few times a month are the most common preferences. TouchBistro 2022: 40% would unsubscribe over too frequent emails. Commercial email and text consent rules apply and are not covered in owner text.

move: Team up with a nearby business, such as a gym or a theater, to trade a small offer for each other's customers.
why: A neighbor's customers already pass your door, and a shared offer reaches them without paying for ads.
watch: Track redemptions with a code or card, and drop partners whose customers never come.
follow_up: Which businesses make good partners?
basis_note: FSR 2017: sell an early reservation with a local theater ticket, offer gym members a perk, and let local groups meet in your space on slow days. Bakers Journal 2015: cross promotions with non competing businesses, such as desserts with a local theater. Advice only, no outcome data.

move: Hand out small samples of 1 item at the door or counter during your quiet hours.
why: Tasting removes the risk of trying something new, and a good sample often turns into a full purchase.
watch: Sample your best seller or a new item rather than leftovers, and count how many tasters buy.
follow_up: How do I sample without giving away too much?
basis_note: Bakers Journal 2015: use sampling events to highlight new items, and suppliers may help pay for samples. Bakers Journal 2013: an open house with free samples and a small gift certificate for a return visit. Trade advice, no sales data found.

move: Put your full menu with prices on your website as text instead of a PDF, so it loads fast and reads well on a phone.
why: Most guests look at the menu online before they visit, and a menu that is hard to read on a phone turns some of them away.
watch: Update the online menu the same day you change prices or dishes.
follow_up: What should my website include?
basis_note: TouchBistro 2024: 85% of US diners look at the menu online before visiting, and Restaurant Dive on TouchBistro 2022 gives 84% (OpenTable users said 86% in 2015). NACS on an MGH survey 2019: 36% were put off ordering because the menu was hard to read, and 56% call a mobile friendly site very important. No source tests PDF against text menus directly.

move: Reply to reviews within a few days, thanking good reviews briefly and answering bad reviews calmly with what you fixed.
why: Future guests read your replies, and a calm fix shows them a problem would be handled well.
watch: Never argue in public or offer deals in a reply, and invite the guest to continue the conversation privately.
follow_up: How do I answer an unfair review?
basis_note: Proserpio and Zervas (Marketing Science, via INFORMS 2017 and HBR 2018): hotels that began responding got 12% more reviews and ratings rose 0.12 stars on average, hotel data. Google review tips: reply professionally and politely, avoid offering deals in replies, and a genuine apology helps.

move: Invite all guests the same way to share honest feedback on review sites that allow requests, and never offer anything in return.
why: An even request adds reviews from ordinary visits, and review sites remove reviews that were rewarded or gathered only from fans.
watch: Check each site's rules, since some ask businesses not to request reviews at all.
follow_up: When is the best time to ask for a review?
basis_note: Google Maps content policy: merchants may encourage genuine reviews but must not offer incentives, selectively solicit positive reviews, or pressure guests on the premises. Yelp: asking for reviews is against its policy and solicited reviews are not recommended. FTC 2022 guide: do not ask only customers you expect to be positive. Asking only happy guests was dropped from the move for this reason.

move: Go through the 50 most recent reviews, list every complaint that shows up more than 2 times, and fix the cause behind the most common.
why: Repeated complaints point to real problems in service or food that are costing you return visits.
watch: Track whether that complaint fades in new reviews over the next few months.
follow_up: What do guests complain about most?
basis_note: Yelp for Business: reviews contain feedback to improve the experience, and 3 reviews in 2 weeks naming the same problem is a signal to investigate. Restaurant Dive 2019 (Zoro data): 82% would avoid a restaurant with dirty bathrooms. No controlled test shows fixes raise ratings.

move: Treat your average star rating as a sales number and go over the newest reviews with your team each month.
why: For independent places, a higher star rating tends to bring in more guests and revenue.
watch: Watch the trend in recent reviews, since old reviews can hide whether things are getting better or worse.
follow_up: How do I raise my star rating?
basis_note: Luca (HBS working paper 12-016): a 1 star increase in Yelp rating led to a 5 to 9% increase in revenue, driven by independent restaurants, with no effect for chains. Seattle 2003 to 2009, Yelp only, effect tied to the rounded star shown. HBS Working Knowledge: ratings settle after 20 or 30 reviews.

move: Check on each table soon after the food arrives with a specific question, so problems get fixed before guests leave.
why: A problem fixed at the table rarely turns into a bad review, while a problem found online is too late to fix.
watch: Ask something specific, like how the steak is cooked, since guests answer a general question with a polite yes.
follow_up: What should I do when a guest is unhappy?
basis_note: Yelp for Business: the best way to avoid critical reviews is to detect and fix problems immediately, with an example of a server catching a lukewarm reaction. Modern Restaurant Management (Ken McGarrie): touch each table between the main course arriving and clearing, ask about a specific dish, and avoid the lazy how is everything.

move: Print a short link or code to your review page on receipts or a small table card.
why: Making a review easy to leave brings in more reviews from ordinary visits.
watch: Keep the wording neutral and ask for honest reviews, so the request never reads as asking only for praise.
follow_up: Which review sites matter most?
basis_note: Google review tips: ask customers to visit a review link or scan a QR code. Google content policy: no pressure on the premises and no selective asking. Yelp allows signs saying you are on Yelp but not requests for reviews, so give every guest the same neutral link.

move: Sell tickets in advance for a special dinner or tasting with a fixed menu and a fixed headcount.
why: Prepaid tickets give you cash up front and an exact count, so you prep precisely and no shows cost you nothing.
watch: Price tickets to cover food, labor and the seats you would have sold otherwise.
follow_up: How do I price a ticketed event?
basis_note: FSR 2015 (Selling Seats): a Chicago fine dining group lost over $260,000 a year to no-shows before ticketing and ran a 1.5% no-show rate after, and its founder (who co-founded a ticketing company) says ticketing suits any restaurant with a check average above $25. WBEZ: a tasting counter requires prepayment so cancellations do not sink a small room. Restaurant Dive 2021: prepaid experiences are a standard no-show tool.

move: Offer your space for private events with a food and drink minimum, and set lower minimums on your slow days.
why: A private event can fill the room in 1 booking, and lower slow day minimums win parties you would otherwise lose.
watch: Put the minimum, deposit and menu in writing so there is no argument on the day.
follow_up: What minimum should I charge for a private event?
basis_note: Tripleseat 2024: minimums run higher on popular dates and lower at off-peak times to attract bookings, built from food, labor and overhead. Tripleseat on dynamic minimums: venues lower minimums to sell a space on an off day. Quill: large group meals like office parties fill slow periods. Vendor guidance, no outcome data.

move: Plan a set menu for the big holidays in your area and take bookings or preorders weeks ahead, with a deposit.
why: A set menu speeds the kitchen on days when demand peaks, and deposits cut no shows when every seat counts.
watch: Open bookings early, keep a waitlist, and plan prep from the confirmed count.
follow_up: Which holidays are worth a special menu?
basis_note: Food Institute 2025 on OpenTable data: experience dining on Mother's Day rose 29% year over year and many families book late. WBEZ: a trattoria lost about 52 of 134 Valentine's Day bookings to cancellations and no-shows. Global News 2017: a $25 no-show charge for large parties solved the problem quickly at a Vancouver restaurant.

move: Host a weekly music, comedy or open mic night on your slow day, at the same time every week.
why: Many diners find live music a draw, and a fixed weekly slot gives people a plan they can repeat.
watch: Give it several weeks, then compare covers and checks on event days with the same day before you started.
follow_up: How do I fill an event night?
basis_note: TouchBistro How Diners Choose Restaurants: live music is a compelling draw for 44% of surveyed diners. Quill: a restaurant hosts open mic and comedy nights for local performers. Trivia and game nights were not found in reputable sources. Music performance licensing is not covered here.

move: Teach a small paid class in your quiet hours, such as bread baking or coffee brewing, and sell your products afterward.
why: Classes earn money from your space and skills when the room is empty, and students often turn into regulars.
watch: Cap the class at what your space handles well, and price it to cover ingredients and staff time.
follow_up: What should I charge for a class?
basis_note: Bakers Journal 2015: announce special events such as a baker demo or cooking classes. Quill: bring in local producers for presentations and tastings during slow periods. Advice only, no revenue data.

move: Before joining a delivery app, work out each item's margin after the commission, which typically runs 15 to 30% of the order.
why: A dish that earns well in the room can barely break even after a commission that size.
example: On a $20 order at a 25% commission, you keep $15 before food and packaging costs.
watch: Count card processing, ads and promotions on top of the commission, since they raise the real cost of each app order.
follow_up: Should I be on delivery apps at all?
basis_note: DoorDash US plans charge 15%, 25% or 30% on delivery (6% on pickup). Uber Eats US charges 20%, 25% or 30% (Lite starts at 15% in some capped cities). ChowNow and Toast both put marketplace commissions at 15 to 30%. Card processing, ads and promotions are extra.

move: Price items on delivery apps above your counter prices to cover the commission and packaging.
why: Matching counter prices means every app order earns less than the same order taken at your register.
watch: Keep the markup modest, and keep app pickup prices equal to your counter, since some apps charge a lower pickup rate for that.
follow_up: How much higher should app prices be?
basis_note: Gordon Haskett data via Food On Demand: 23 of 25 chains priced app menus higher, average premium 19% (quick service 26%, casual 11%). DoorDash says markups can mean up to 37% fewer sales and 78% lower reorders, its own data and it favors price parity. The 6% DoorDash and 7% Uber Eats pickup rates require in store pricing.

move: Offer your own online ordering for pickup, and point regulars to it on receipts, bag inserts, signs and your website.
why: Direct orders keep the commission with you and let you reach those guests again.
watch: Make your own ordering as easy as the apps, or guests will keep using the apps.
follow_up: How do I get guests to order direct?
basis_note: Toast support checklist: add order online buttons on your site and wherever guests search. ChowNow: slip a card in delivery bags with a 1st direct order offer, and track direct vs marketplace share. Restaurant Dive (William Blair data): more consumers prefer ordering directly from the restaurant than through marketplaces. Direct ordering still carries processing and software fees.

move: Before listing a dish for delivery, let it sit wrapped for 30 minutes and taste it, and leave off anything that fails.
why: Soggy or cold food brings bad ratings and refunds that cost more than the sale.
watch: Order your own delivery now and then and eat it at home to see what guests get.
follow_up: Which dishes travel badly?
basis_note: DoorDash off premise guide: you probably should not put every item on the delivery menu, test by wrapping a dish in foil for 30 minutes and tasting it. Restaurant Dive 2019 quoting Uber Eats: successful delivery menus typically run 15 to 20 items and can differ from the dine in menu.

move: Use vented containers for crispy food and pack sauces and dressings on the side.
why: Good packaging keeps food closer to how it left the kitchen, which protects ratings and repeat orders.
watch: Build the packaging cost into the delivery price, since better containers cost more.
follow_up: Which packaging keeps fries crispy?
basis_note: DoorDash guides: vent hot containers, bag hot and cold separately, pack sauces and dressings separately so food does not go soggy. NRA 2025 off premises report: 90% of off premises customers would likely order more variety with better packaging. Better packaging costs more.

move: Offer a takeout bundle that feeds a family, such as a main, 2 sides and a dessert, at 1 set price.
why: Bundles raise the order size and are easy for the kitchen to prep in batches.
example: A $45 bundle replacing 4 separate $9 meals adds $9 to the order.
watch: Build bundles from items you already prep in volume.
follow_up: How should I price a family bundle?
basis_note: Restaurant Dive 2020 citing NPD: family and larger party visits at quick service raised average check 5%. NRA 2025 announcement: 67% of consumers are interested in bundled meals. DoorDash: bundles such as a family style meal make ordering easier for guests and kitchens. Mostly chain data.

move: Pause or slow online orders when the kitchen is slammed, and quote pickup times you can actually hit.
why: Late orders bring bad ratings and refunds, and they slow down the guests already in your room.
watch: Use the busy setting to add prep time before you pause completely, so guests still see an honest time.
follow_up: How do I balance delivery with dine in?
basis_note: Toast support: you can delay or snooze online orders, and guests see the later quoted time. DoorDash merchant help: add prep time or pause orders by channel. Uber Eats: Busy Mode adds minutes and updates guest estimates. No source covers how frequent pausing affects app ranking.

move: Add a clear photo and a short description to every item on your delivery and online menus.
why: Guests ordering on a phone cannot see or smell the food, so photos and plain descriptions help them choose.
watch: Shoot real dishes in good daylight, and update photos whenever a dish changes.
follow_up: What makes a good delivery menu photo?
basis_note: DoorDash merchant blog: item photos linked to up to 44% higher monthly sales and descriptions to up to 18% more, platform reported figures. Uber Eats: listings with photos sell better, descriptions of 140 to 260 characters work best.

move: If you serve alcohol, count bar stock weekly and work out pour cost for spirits, beer and wine separately.
why: Most bars aim for an overall pour cost near 18 to 24%, with spirits running lowest and wine highest, so a number above that points to waste or pricing.
watch: Compare each category with its own range, since a blended bar number hides where the loss is.
follow_up: How do I stop overpouring?
basis_note: Overall pour cost of 18 to 24% appears in Backbar, BinWise, the DoorDash merchant blog and Restaurant365, with spirits near 15%, draft beer near 20% and bottled beer near 25%. Wine is disputed: Backbar, BinWise and DoorDash say 30 to 40%, BevSpot customer medians put it at 28% and its targets at 22%.

move: If you pour wine by the glass, set each glass price near what the whole bottle costs you wholesale.
why: Opened bottles can turn before they are finished, and this pricing protects your margin when some goes unsold.
example: A bottle that costs you $12 sells by the glass at $12, so 5 glasses bring in $60.
watch: Track how much opened wine you pour out, and shorten the by the glass list if waste is high.
follow_up: How many wines should I pour by the glass?
basis_note: PUNCH: a glass is generally priced at the wholesale price of the bottle. VinePair: common in US sommelier training but not universal, some price from a margin target and charge more for wines that spoil fast. BevSpot: same rule, roughly a 20 to 25% pour cost on glasses.

move: If you have a bar, measure every pour with a jigger or a metered spout, and spot check pours during service.
why: Free pours tend to run over, and small extra pours across a week add up to bottles you never charge for.
example: An extra 0.25 ounce on 400 drinks a week is 100 ounces, about 4 bottles.
watch: Present the change to bartenders as consistency for guests, and check pour cost again after a month.
follow_up: What pour cost should my bar run?
basis_note: DoorDash merchant blog: set a pour policy and use pour spouts and jiggers. Restaurant365: enforcing measured pours with no exceptions is among the most effective ways to cut liquor loss. StarChefs: a bar trimmed a pour by 0.5 ounce to hit a 20% cost target.

move: Add 2 or 3 house made nonalcoholic drinks made with the same care as your other drinks, and price them as real drinks.
why: More guests now drink less or not at all, and a well made nonalcoholic drink earns money from guests who would otherwise order water.
watch: Cost each recipe, since fresh juices and nonalcoholic spirits can cost as much as liquor.
follow_up: What should I charge for a mocktail?
basis_note: NRA 2026 What is Hot forecast: rise of low and no alcohol drinks. NIQ 2025: nonalcoholic retail sales up 22% year over year. Square: guests will pay a similar price for well made mocktails. Margins are disputed, a Boston Globe 2026 report quotes an operator calling mocktail margins less than ideal.

move: Cost every drink on your board, counting beans, milk, syrup and the cup, and price each so it covers those with room to spare.
why: Milk, syrups and cups add up drink by drink, and a popular drink priced by guesswork can quietly earn very little.
watch: Recost drinks whenever milk, bean or cup prices change.
follow_up: What should a latte cost me to make?
basis_note: Square: drink cost of goods includes beans, milk, syrups and the cup. Perfect Daily Grind (consultant Chris Deferio) puts drink cost of goods at 15 to 25%, while 7shifts says most shops target 25 to 35% on beverages, so no range is given to owners.

move: Use a steady, moderately priced blend for milk and flavored drinks, and save your priciest beans for straight espresso and filter.
why: Milk and syrup cover the finer notes of expensive beans, so a solid blend holds cost down where guests will not taste the difference.
watch: Taste the blend in your most popular milk drink before switching, since a flat blend can hurt your best seller.
follow_up: How do I choose a house blend?
basis_note: Perfect Daily Grind 2025: shops use consistent, moderately priced coffees for flavored and milk drinks and keep higher scoring origin coffees for espresso and filter, since blends hold up to syrups and control ingredient cost.
