move: Pull sales by hour for each day of the week from your POS and mark the blocks that sit well below the rest.
why: Seeing your empty hours tells you where an offer or a schedule change will pay, instead of guessing.
watch: Tackle 1 weak block at a time so you can tell what moved it.
follow_up: What can I do with my slowest hours?
basis_note: FSR 2022: summarize daily and hourly sales by day of week and offer specials during slow times. SpotOn: if sales consistently dip in a 2 hour window, cut staffing there. Working 1 block at a time is our own pacing advice.

move: Give your afternoon lull its own offer, like a coffee and pastry deal or a small snack menu, at a set time each day.
why: Afternoon guests lean toward snacks and cold drinks, and a simple offer turns empty hours into sales while staff are already on.
watch: Keep the offer simple enough to run with a small crew.
follow_up: What sells well in the afternoon?
basis_note: Circana 2026: afternoon snack traffic expected to edge up 2% over 3 years. NACS citing the WSJ: a big coffee chain is pushing afternoon drinks and snacks, and Technomic says later in the day people shift to iced and sparkling drinks. Placer.ai: quick service shows afternoon strength.

move: If your area has people out and about in late morning on their days off, test a short brunch menu on 1 of those days.
why: Brunch draws guests at hours when your room may be closed or empty, and breakfast staples cost relatively little to make.
watch: Build the menu from ingredients you already stock, and staff lightly until the crowd builds.
follow_up: What should a brunch menu include?
basis_note: Marketplace 2024: brunch carries better margins and breakfast staples are not especially expensive (Technomic: 70% order alcohol at brunch). FSR 2023: reuse dinner ingredients, complexity is the enemy. Square: brunch margins can be finicky and weekend brunch strains staff. Weaker economics without alcohol.

move: Set up a grab and go case near the door with ready items for morning guests in a hurry.
why: Ready items need no work during the rush and let commuters buy without waiting at the counter.
watch: Make only what sells by close, and track leftovers each day to set amounts.
follow_up: What sells best in a grab and go case?
basis_note: 7shifts coffee guide: grab and go items need no prep during service and often carry strong margins. Placer.ai 2025: 14.6% of coffee visits happen before 8am. Unsold items are waste.

move: If you count on office lunch traffic, track lunch covers by weekday and put your lunch specials and staff on the days offices are fullest.
why: Many office workers now come in only some days, so lunch demand bunches up on those days.
watch: Recheck the pattern every few months, since office schedules keep shifting.
follow_up: How do I attract office lunch crowds?
basis_note: Restaurant Dive 2024 (Dinova CEO): hybrid workers are mostly in the office Tuesday through Thursday. NRN 2025 citing Circana: office occupancy averaged 52% in 2025. No source covers an express lunch format, so that idea was dropped.

move: Offer catering for nearby offices and meetings, ordered a day ahead and prepped during your quiet hours.
why: Catering adds large orders without using seats, and the prep fits into hours when staff are already on.
example: A $300 catering order each week adds $15,600 in a year.
watch: Price in packaging and delivery time, and set a minimum order size.
follow_up: How do I start catering?
basis_note: Restaurant Dive 2024: about 54% of restaurants planned to add catering, and catering platforms report interest from many small restaurants. NRN 2024: independents and small chains are ramping up catering for higher margin sales and better labor use. Examples are mostly chains.

move: Before adding a new daypart, test it on 2 or 3 days a week for a set period with a short menu.
why: A new daypart costs labor and prep before it has a crowd, and a short test limits the loss if it does not catch on.
watch: Decide in advance what sales would count as success, so hope does not keep a losing daypart open.
follow_up: How long should I test a new daypart?
basis_note: Square: test kitchen setup and staffing before launching brunch, it takes fine tuning. Toast support: ease into a new channel on a slower day. FSR: stick to your strengths and reuse ingredients. The pilot idea is inferred from these, no controlled test was found.

move: Check the forecast each morning and adjust prep and staffing for rain, heat or snow.
why: Weather shifts walk ins and delivery in patterns you can learn, and planning for it cuts both waste and short staffing.
watch: Note sales on bad weather days so you learn your own pattern.
follow_up: How does weather change my sales?
basis_note: Restaurant Dive 2019 on Ohio State (Bujisic): temperature was the top weather factor at 1 restaurant, rain did not cut sales there, combine POS with weather data to forecast. 7shifts: weather effects vary by concept. UGA climate blog: quick service is less weather sensitive than casual dining. Effects differ by venue, so the move says learn your own pattern.

move: On rainy days, tell staff before service that guests may arrive in a worse mood, and add a small comfort like upbeat music or a warm drink.
why: Guests are more likely to leave a harsh review on a rainy day, and small comforts help the visit end well.
watch: Compare review scores on rainy days with dry days over a season to see whether the extra care helps.
follow_up: How do I keep guests happy in bad weather?
basis_note: Ohio State (Bujisic and Bogicevic, Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Research): the odds of very negative versus very positive comments were 2.9 times greater on rainy days, and the researchers suggest briefing staff and offering a free drink or upbeat music.

move: Keep a staffing plan for days the patio is open and another for days it is closed, and pick from the forecast each morning.
why: Patio seats are often your most profitable space in good weather, and staffing them on a washout day wastes labor.
watch: Have a plan for moving patio guests inside when a storm hits during service.
follow_up: How do I staff for the patio?
basis_note: Push Operations 2026: the patio is the most profitable square footage when the weather cooperates, keep separate patio open and patio closed labor templates. Rosnet: forecast patio staffing from past summers. No source on heaters or shade was found, so that idea was dropped.

move: Run a limited time seasonal item for a few weeks, and announce its end date when you launch it.
why: Guests see seasonal items as special, which brings regulars back and lets the item carry a healthy price.
watch: Build it from ingredients you already stock where possible, since each new item adds waste risk.
follow_up: How long should a seasonal special run?
basis_note: 7shifts coffee guide: seasonal offerings often become high margin items because guests see them as special. NRA 2025 announcement: nearly 9 in 10 consumers would use limited time offers. Limited time items add stock and waste risk.

move: Use your slow season for deep cleaning, menu testing and training, and set cash aside in busy months to carry you through it.
why: Slow months are predictable, and doing that work when it costs you fewer sales protects the busy months.
watch: Check last year's sales by month so you know when your slow stretch starts.
follow_up: How do I prepare for the slow season?
basis_note: NRN 2019 citing NPD: January traffic ran 6% below the average month. Restaurant Association of New Zealand: use downtime for staff development, deep cleaning, maintenance and recipe testing. Sculpture Hospitality: the slow season must be planned and budgeted, save part of profits in strong months.

move: In the holiday season, give a bonus card with each gift card bought, valid only in your slow months.
why: You collect cash in a busy month and bring guests back in quiet months, when they usually spend beyond the bonus.
example: With 100 cards sold at $50 plus a $10 bonus each, you take in $5,000 now against $1,000 of bonus visits later.
watch: Mark the bonus card clearly as promotional with its valid dates, and track how many come back.
follow_up: When should I start selling gift cards?
basis_note: NRN 2019: a taco chain gave a bonus card with each $25 gift card bought through December, redeemable in January, gift card sales rose 51% and bonus redemptions brought 4,400 January visits. NRN 2022: nearly 50% of gift card sales come in the last 2 months, about 40% of redemptions in January to March, and guests tend to spend beyond card value. CFPB rule 1005.20 says promotional cards must be labeled as such and show the expiry.

move: On hot days, move iced drinks and cold items to the top of your board, and have extra ice and cold brew ready.
why: Heat changes what guests want, and being ready catches sales you would lose to slow service.
watch: Note which items jump on hot days so next time you prep the right amounts.
follow_up: What sells best on hot days?
basis_note: Perfect Daily Grind 2025: cold drinks are over 75% of a big chain US drink sales and concentrates make iced lattes much faster. UGA climate blog: coffee shops see slightly more traffic on very hot days. Restaurant Dive on Bujisic: heavy items sell less in heat.

move: Make sure every guest is acknowledged within moments of walking in, even with a nod and a quick word when the team is slammed.
why: Guests accept a wait far more easily when they know they have been seen.
watch: Watch the door at your busiest hour, and assign someone to it if guests stand there unnoticed.
follow_up: How do I make guests feel welcome?
basis_note: Maister: waits before service feel longer than waits during it, and a quick word that guests have been seen eases the wait. Noone et al. (Cornell 2007): delays before ordering upset guests more than delays during the meal, though fine dining guests do not want the welcome rushed. Epos Now (vendor): greet guests as they arrive, with a nod and a quick word when busy.

move: When something goes wrong, own it, apologize, fix it fast, and then add a small extra the guest did not expect.
why: A mistake handled generously can win a guest back, and it often decides whether they return or post a bad review.
watch: Match the extra to the size of the mistake, and log what went wrong so repeat problems get fixed at the source.
follow_up: What should I comp when something goes wrong?
basis_note: Danny Meyer (Global Leadership Network 2018, KQED 2006): be aware, acknowledge, apologize, act, then add additional generosity, and write a great last chapter. AlleyWatch on the 5 A's: no alibis, and the extra should match the mistake.

move: Manage 95% of your spending tightly, and treat a small slice, around 5%, as a budget for surprising guests.
why: Tight control everywhere else pays for the moments guests remember, and those moments bring them back and get you talked about.
watch: Track what you spend on gestures so the slice stays small.
follow_up: What kinds of surprises work best?
basis_note: Will Guidara (McKinsey Author Talks 2022): manage money tightly 95% of the time so that 5% of the time you can spend foolishly on guests. US Foods on Unreasonable Hospitality: be hard nosed about 95% of expenses, then splurge where guests feel it. Rule of thumb, no payback data.

move: Train staff to listen for small details, like a guest mentioning a birthday or a dish they miss, and act on them with a small gesture.
why: Personal gestures cost little, and guests remember them long after the meal, which brings them back.
watch: Keep gestures personal and occasional, since a scripted freebie for everyone stops feeling special.
follow_up: How do I train staff to notice details?
basis_note: Unreasonable Hospitality (Commoncog case, CNBC 2022, NRN 2024): staff built small personal gestures, called legends, from details they overheard, such as serving a street hot dog to guests who had never had 1, and a dedicated role helped staff carry them out. Fine dining origin, so scale it down.

move: Pace each table to its situation, moving briskly when guests are on a lunch break and letting dinner guests set the tempo.
why: Guests on a break welcome speed, but rushing a relaxed meal hurts satisfaction, and the right pace frees seats without upsetting anyone.
watch: When it is unclear, ask guests whether they are short on time instead of guessing.
follow_up: How do I train servers to read tables?
basis_note: Noone et al. (Cornell 2007, 218 diners): a fast pace before ordering was fine at lunch but not at dinner, fine dining guests were most sensitive, and rushing the meal itself cut satisfaction. Guidara (McKinsey 2022): tailor service to each guest and ask about preferences. The reason for dining did not change the pace effect, so the move keys on lunch vs dinner and on asking.

move: Make the goodbye as warm as the welcome, with a thank you at the door and, now and then, a small treat to take home.
why: Guests remember the end of a visit strongly, so a good finish lifts how they rate the whole experience.
watch: Keep paying and leaving quick, since a slow check can spoil a good meal at the last step.
follow_up: What small treats work as a send off?
basis_note: Richard Chase (co-author of HBR 2001 on behavioral science in service, interviewed by Computerworld): finish strong, since people anchor on the last part of an encounter. Guidara (Unreasonable Hospitality excerpt): a stumble at the end can undo the goodwill of a meal. Noone et al.: guests appreciate a fast check settlement.

move: Add up food, drink and labor costs every week and divide by sales to get your prime cost percentage.
why: Prime cost is the biggest share of what you can control, and most restaurants aim to keep it between 55 and 65% of sales.
watch: Look at the trend across weeks, since 1 bad week can simply reflect when deliveries landed.
follow_up: Where should I start cutting costs?
basis_note: Restaurant365: target about 60%, full service 60 to 65%, quick service 55 to 60%, weekly review is the standard. MarketMan: most operators should keep it between 55 and 65%. Square (operator Ming-Tai Huh): under 65%. NRA 2025: limited service median prime cost was 65 cents per sales dollar, at the top of the band.

move: Each year, divide your total card fees by card sales to get your effective rate, and compare it with other processors' offers.
why: Card fees take a slice of nearly every sale, and a small difference in rate adds up over a year.
example: Cutting your rate by 0.3% on $500,000 of card sales saves $1,500 a year.
watch: Compare the total effective rate, since a low headline rate can hide monthly and per transaction fees.
follow_up: How do I compare card processing offers?
basis_note: US Chamber CO: typical card fees run 1.5 to 3.5% plus a flat fee, request quotes from several providers, interchange plus pricing is most transparent. Square: check statements for fee changes, card not present costs more, average cost cited at 2.87 to 4.35%. Ranges differ at the edges, so no number is given to owners.

move: Turn on cooking equipment on a schedule as service needs it, instead of switching everything on at opening.
why: Ovens, fryers and grills left idling burn energy all day without cooking anything you sell.
watch: Post startup and shutdown times on each piece of equipment so every shift follows them.
follow_up: How else can I cut energy costs?
basis_note: ENERGY STAR guide for cafes and restaurants (with the PG&E Food Service Technology Center): use a startup and shutdown plan, cutting idle time saves about $200 to $1,000 a year per appliance. ENERGY STAR small business page: saving 20% on energy can raise profit by as much as 33%.

move: Swap an old pre rinse spray valve for a low flow model, and get dripping faucets fixed right away.
why: The dish station uses a lot of hot water, so saving water also cuts the energy spent heating it.
watch: Check that the new valve still cleans well, or staff will just rinse longer.
follow_up: Where else am I wasting water?
basis_note: EPA WaterSense: replace spray valves flowing 1.6 gallons a minute or more, saving over 7,000 gallons and $110 to $200 a year, spray valves can be nearly 1/3 of kitchen water use. ENERGY STAR guide: fixing leaks in sinks and dish machines can save about $1,000 a year.

move: Check how full your dumpster is at each pickup, and ask your hauler for a smaller bin or fewer pickups if it often goes out with room to spare.
why: You pay for hauling capacity whether or not you fill it, and cutting food waste can shrink that cost further.
watch: Recheck after busy seasons so the bin still fits your volume.
follow_up: Which fixed costs can I lower?
basis_note: EPA Region 9 guide: businesses may be able to reduce dumpster size or pickup frequency, and diverting food scraps cut hauling cost 30% in 1 case. ReFED: negotiate hauler contracts and ask about food waste recycling. No source covered rebidding linen or pest services, so that idea was dropped.

move: Review comps, voids and discounts in your POS each week, by staff member and by reason.
why: Unexplained comps and voids are a common way money leaks out, and watching POS data closely tends to cut theft.
watch: Have the POS ask for a reason on every void and comp, and remember many voids are honest mistakes that point to training needs.
follow_up: What level of comps is normal?
basis_note: Restaurant365: track comps and voids by reason and by employee, have managers record why, and check whether most voids land on cash checks, voids also flag staff who need training. Washington University news story on Pierce, Snow and McAfee (Management Science 2015): POS based theft monitoring at 392 restaurants cut theft 22% and lifted revenue about 7%.

move: Clean refrigeration condenser coils on a schedule and check door gaskets for gaps.
why: Dirty coils and worn seals make refrigeration run harder, which raises energy bills and the risk of a costly breakdown.
watch: Write the cleaning date on each unit so it never gets skipped.
follow_up: What maintenance saves the most money?
basis_note: ENERGY STAR guide: clean evaporator and condenser coils and replace worn door gaskets, proper maintenance cuts energy cost and prevents costly failures, leaky gaskets waste money every month. ENERGY STAR small business page: tune up HVAC yearly.
